mainTopic: A borrowed ox's liability, change of custody, and whether a stadium ox may be a קרבן
overview: The amud continues the case of a borrowed ox that turned out to be a מועד, where the borrower and the owner each pay half the damage. The גמרא asks why the borrower pays at all, since with a תם he could have admitted or hidden the ox. It answers that the court seized the ox first. It then defends the owner's half through a series of claims and counter-claims, ending with רבי נתן's rule that a creditor can collect directly from his debtor's debtor. Next, the רישא and סיפא of the ברייתא seem to disagree about whether a change of custody changes an ox's status. רבי יוחנן, רבה and רב פפא each resolve this differently. The גמרא then asks whether a שור האצטדין that killed a person may be brought as a קרבן: רב says כשר, שמואל says פסול. A ברייתא seems to challenge שמואל, but the גמרא shows that its line about a forced goring refers to putting the ox to death. Finally, the גמרא asks why the owner of a רובע pays no כופר, and אביי begins an answer that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The borrower could have admitted and gone free
steps.stepSummary: The borrower argues: had the ox really been a תם, I could have admitted the damage and been exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it were a תם, I would have admitted it, and I would have been exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is continuing its challenge to the ruling that the borrower pays half the damage. It gives the borrower a claim: with a תם, I had a way out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Half-damage for a תם is treated here as a קנס, a fine. Someone who admits on his own to something that carries a fine is exempt. So if the ox had been a תם, the borrower could have admitted and paid nothing. Why should he pay half now?

keyTerms.meaning: An ox with no history of goring; its owner pays only half the damage
A fine, a payment set by the תורה that is more or less than the actual loss
One who admits to something carrying a fine is exempt from paying it

phrases.english: If it were a תם, I would have admitted it,
and I would have been exempt!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the challenge from before this section against the borrower paying half
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the borrower pays half the damage
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Half-damage of a תם is a קנס, and admitting to a קנס exempts you, so with a תם the borrower would have paid nothing

steps.title: Even if half-damage is regular money, he could have hidden the ox
steps.stepSummary: Even according to the view that half-damage is ordinary money and not a fine, the borrower could have hidden a תם in the marsh.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even according to the one who says half-damage is ordinary money, let him say to him: if it were a תם, I would have hidden it away in the marsh!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא strengthens the challenge so that it works for both views about half-damage. Even if admitting would not help, the borrower had another way out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Damage from a תם is paid only from the body of the ox itself. If the borrower hid the ox, the injured person would have nothing to collect from. A מועד is paid from all of one's property, so hiding the ox would not help, and that is why the borrower lost his escape route.

keyTerms.meaning: The view that half-damage is ordinary money owed, not a fine
I would have smuggled away
A marsh, a place to hide the animal

phrases.english: And even according to the one who says
half-damage is ordinary money,
let him say to him:
if it were a תם,
I would have smuggled it away to the marsh!
phrases.notes: A תם is paid only from the ox itself, so with no ox there is nothing to collect.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲפִילּוּ לְמַאן דְּאָמַר פַּלְגָא נִזְקָא מָמוֹנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the challenge of step 1 to the other view of half-damage
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the borrower pays half the damage
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A תם is paid only from its own body, so hiding it would have freed the borrower

steps.title: The court seized the ox first
steps.stepSummary: The case is one where the court grabbed the ox before the borrower could admit or hide it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what are we dealing with here? A case where the court got there first and seized it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the case of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the court had already taken the ox, the borrower could not have admitted first or hidden the animal. Neither escape route was open to him, so his claim 'with a תם I'd have gone free' does not work. Therefore he pays half.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a case)
The court
It seized it

phrases.english: Rather, what are we dealing with here?
A case where the court got there first,
and seized it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenges of steps 1 and 2
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The borrower always had a way to avoid paying for a תם, so he should not pay
steps.terutzMaskana: The court seized the ox before he could admit or hide it, so he had no escape and pays half

steps.title: Then why should the owner pay?
steps.stepSummary: If the court seized the ox, the owner can blame the borrower for letting it fall into the court's hands.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why do the owners pay half-damage? Let him say to him: you let my ox be seized by someone I cannot argue the case with!
steps.whatsHappening: The answer just given creates a new problem, and the גמרא now challenges the owner's half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner can say: the court collects exactly what is owed, and I cannot negotiate a compromise with it. Since the borrower let the ox get seized, he should carry the whole loss. So why does the owner pay anything?

keyTerms.meaning: If so (a challenge built on the previous answer)
The owners of the ox
To argue a case, to negotiate a legal claim

phrases.english: If so,
why do the owners pay half the damage?
Let him say to him: you let my ox be seized
in the hands of someone I cannot
phrases.notes: The letter in square brackets is part of the corrected wording.

phrases.english: argue the case with!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, בְּעָלִים אַמַּאי מְשַׁלְּמִים חֲצִי נֶזֶק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 3 from the owner's side
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the owner pays half, given the case of step 3
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The borrower caused the ox to be seized by an unbending court, so he should bear the full loss

steps.title: The court would have taken it from the owner anyway
steps.stepSummary: The borrower answers: if I had returned the ox to you, the court would have taken it from you.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he can say to him: if I had returned it to you, wouldn't they have taken it from you?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers why the owner still pays his half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower did not cause the owner any real loss. The ox did the damage, and the court would have seized it from the owner just the same. So the owner cannot blame the borrower for the court's seizure.

keyTerms.meaning: I had returned it
They take, they would take

steps.whatToRemember: The borrower pays half because the court seized the ox before he could admit or hide it. The owner pays half because the court would have taken the ox from him anyway.

phrases.english: Because he can say to him:
if I had returned it to you,
wouldn't they have taken it from you?!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ: אִי אַהְדַּרְתֵּיהּ נִיהֲלָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 4
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The borrower caused the owner a loss by letting the court seize the ox
steps.terutzMaskana: The court would have seized it from the owner anyway, so the owner pays his half

steps.title: The owner says he would have hidden the ox
steps.stepSummary: The owner pushes back: if you had returned the ox to me, I would have smuggled it to the marsh and the court could not have seized it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let the owner say to him: If you had returned it to me, I would have hidden it in the marsh!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the borrower's answer from Step 5 by giving the owner a comeback. The owner claims he would have hidden the ox before the court could take it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 5 the borrower said the court would have taken the ox from the owner anyway. The owner now argues that this is not true, because he would have hidden it. If that works, the borrower really did cause him a loss.

keyTerms.meaning: You had returned it
I would have smuggled away or hidden
The marsh, a hiding place where the court could not find the ox

phrases.english: But let him say to him:
phrases.notes: Here the owner is the one speaking to the borrower.

phrases.english: If you had returned it to me,
I would have smuggled it to the marsh!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the borrower's defense in Step 5
steps.kashyaTarget: The borrower's claim that the court would have taken the ox from the owner anyway
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The owner could have hidden the ox, so the borrower's failure to return it is what caused the loss.

steps.title: Hiding the ox would not have helped
steps.stepSummary: The borrower answers that the injured party would have been paid from the owner's best property anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he can say to him: In the end, wouldn't they have been paid from your best-quality property?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the owner's comeback. Hiding the ox would not have saved the owner any money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Damage done by a מועד is not paid only from the ox itself. It is collected from the owner's other property, even his best land. So hiding the ox would not have protected the owner, and the borrower caused no real loss.

keyTerms.meaning: In the end, either way
Best-quality property
They would be paid

phrases.english: Because he can say to him:
phrases.notes: Now the borrower answers the owner.

phrases.aramaic: סוֹף סוֹף, לָאו מֵעֲלִיָּיה הֲווֹ מִשְׁתַּלְּמִי?!
phrases.english: In the end, wouldn't they have been paid from the best-quality property?!
phrases.notes: He means the injured party would have collected from the owner's other assets, not just from the ox.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 6
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the claimed loss would have happened anyway
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Hiding the ox would have spared the owner from paying.
steps.terutzMaskana: A מועד pays from the owner's other property, so hiding the ox would not have helped.

steps.title: What if the owner has no other property?
steps.stepSummary: The answer works only if the owner owns other property. If he has none, hiding the ox would have saved him.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well where he has property. Where he has no property, what is there to say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a gap in the answer of Step 7. If the owner owns nothing besides the ox, hiding it really would have protected him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 depended on the injured party being able to collect from other property. Without other property, the ox is the only thing that can be collected. So in that case the borrower did cause a loss by not returning it.

keyTerms.meaning: This works out well
Property or assets
What is there to say?

phrases.english: This works well where he has property,
phrases.notes: He means the owner, who might own other assets besides the ox.

phrases.english: but where he has no property,
what is there to say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the answer of Step 7 to one kind of case
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that payment would come from the owner's best property
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the owner has no other property, hiding the ox would have saved him, so the borrower did cause a loss.

steps.title: The borrower is directly obligated to the injured party
steps.stepSummary: The borrower says: just as I owe you, I also owe the injured party, based on רבי נתן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he can say to him: Just as I am obligated to you, so too I am obligated to that other person. This is based on רבי נתן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer that works even when the owner has no other property. The borrower says the court could rightly take the ox from him for the injured party.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower owes the owner the ox, and the owner owes the injured party. Under רבי נתן's rule, the injured party can collect straight from the borrower. So the court taking the ox from the borrower was proper, and the borrower is not to blame.

keyTerms.meaning: I am obligated or bound as a debtor
To that other person, the injured party

steps.whyThisMatters: This brings in the principle known as שעבודא דרבי נתן: a creditor can collect directly from his debtor's debtor.

phrases.english: Because he can say to him:
Just as I am obligated to you,
phrases.notes: He means he must return the ox to the owner.

phrases.english: so too I am obligated to that one,
because of the ruling of רבי נתן.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ: כִּי הֵיכָא דְּמִשְׁתַּעְבַּדְנָא לְדִידָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 8
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings in a new legal principle that covers every case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without other property, the borrower caused the owner a loss.
steps.terutzMaskana: The borrower is directly obligated to the injured party through רבי נתן's rule, so the seizure was proper.

steps.title: The source for רבי נתן's rule
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי נתן: if A is owed money by B, and B is owed money by C, the court collects from C and pays A, based on a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: רבי נתן says: From where do we know that if one lends his friend a מנה, and that friend lends another, we take from this one and give to that one? The verse says: 'And he shall give it to the one to whom he is guilty.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא that is the source for רבי נתן's rule used in Step 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי נתן says that money owed down a chain can be collected directly, skipping the middleman. He learns this from the פסוק about returning stolen property, which says to give it to the one to whom he is liable. Here the borrower is the last debtor in the chain, the owner is the middleman, and the injured party is the first creditor.

keyTerms.meaning: A creditor, someone owed money
A sum of one hundred זוז
The verse teaches

steps.whatToRemember: Under רבי נתן's rule, a creditor can collect straight from his debtor's debtor. That is why the borrower is not blamed when the court takes the ox from him for the injured party.

phrases.english: As it was taught: רבי נתן says:
From where do we know, for one who is owed a מנה by his friend,
and his friend is owed by his friend,
phrases.notes: So there is a chain: A is owed by B, and B is owed by C.

phrases.english: from where do we know that we take from this one and give to that one?
phrases.notes: The court takes from C and pays A directly.

phrases.english: The verse teaches:
"And he shall give it to the one to whom he is guilty."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for the rule used in Step 9
steps.raayaObject: The rule that a creditor can collect directly from his debtor's debtor
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא of רבי נתן, learned from במדבר 5:7

steps.title: The last clause: an ox that became forewarned at the borrower's house
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the סיפא of the ברייתא. An ox became a מועד with the borrower and was returned. The owner pays only half damage, and the borrower pays nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the ox became forewarned while at the borrower's house, and he gave it back to the owner, then if it gores, the owner pays half the damage and the borrower pays nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the last part of the ברייתא it quoted earlier. It is setting up a question that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ox gored three times while with the borrower, so it became a מועד there. Once it is back with its owner, it is treated like a תם again: the owner pays only חצי נזק. The borrower, who no longer has the ox, owes nothing at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Became a מוּעָד (an ox with a known pattern of goring), which pays full damage
A borrower
The owner
Half the damage, which is what a תָּם (an ox without a pattern) pays
Exempt from paying anything

phrases.english: It was made forewarned in the borrower's house,
and he returned it to the owner –
the owner pays half the damage,
and the borrower is exempt from anything.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the רבי נתן discussion back to another clause of the ברייתא about the borrowed ox.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An ox made מועד in the borrower's custody and then returned to the owner pays only חצי נזק, and the borrower is fully exempt.

steps.title: The first and last clauses seem to contradict each other
steps.stepSummary: The סיפא implies that a change of custody changes the ox's status. The רישא implies that it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: The last clause shows that changing who holds the ox changes its status, but the first clause shows that changing who holds it does not change its status!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the two halves of the same ברייתא seem to follow opposite rules.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the סיפא, the ox becomes a תם again once it moves back to the owner, so a new custody seems to 'reset' its status. In the רישא, the ox kept its מועד status even after it was lent out, so a new custody did not reset it. One ברייתא cannot hold both rules.

keyTerms.meaning: The last clause of a teaching
The first clause of a teaching
A change of custody changes the ox's status

steps.confusionAlert: Here רְשׁוּת does not mean 'permission.' It means 'domain' or 'custody': whose hands the ox is in.

phrases.english: The last clause – custody changes [the status],
the first clause – custody does not change [the status]!

steps.triggerLanguage: סֵיפָא – רְשׁוּת מְשַׁנָּה, רֵישָׁא – רְשׁוּת אֵינָהּ מְשַׁנָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the clause just quoted by setting it against the רישא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The internal consistency of the ברייתא's רישא and סיפא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The רישא keeps the ox's status despite a change of custody, while the סיפא resets the status after a change of custody. These are opposite rules inside one source.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the two clauses come from different תנאים
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says the ברייתא is 'broken.' One תנא taught the רישא and a different תנא taught the סיפא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: This ברייתא is broken. Whoever taught this part did not teach that part.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers the contradiction by saying the two clauses do not come from the same person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן does not try to make the clauses agree. One תנא holds that custody does not change the status (the רישא). Another תנא holds that it does (the סיפא). Since they are two opinions, the contradiction goes away.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Break it': the ברייתא is split between two authors

keyTerms.term: מִי שֶׁשָּׁנָה זוֹ לֹא שָׁנָה זוֹ
keyTerms.meaning: The one who taught this clause did not teach that one

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Break it;
phrases.notes: 'Break it' means the ברייתא isn't one smooth teaching. It's put together from two sources.

phrases.aramaic: מִי שֶׁשָּׁנָה זוֹ לֹא שָׁנָה זוֹ.
phrases.english: the one who taught this did not teach that.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the source between two authors
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The whole ברייתא is from one תנא, so its clauses contradict.
steps.terutzMaskana: The רישא and סיפא come from two תנאים who argue about whether custody changes the ox's status.

steps.title: רבה: custody never changes the status, but the owner can reject the borrower's effect
steps.stepSummary: רבה keeps the ברייתא as one teaching. Both clauses hold that custody does not change the status. In the סיפא, the owner tells the borrower he had no right to make the ox a מועד.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Since the first clause holds that custody does not change the status, the last clause also holds that custody does not change the status. The reason for the last clause is that the owner can say to the borrower: 'It is not up to you to make my ox a מועד.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives a different answer from רבי יוחנן's, one that keeps both clauses together under one rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבה, the רישא shows the basic rule: a change of custody does not change the ox's status. The סיפא is not about custody at all. It is about the owner's claim. The ox became a מועד through the borrower, and the owner says the borrower had no power to give his ox that status, so the owner pays only half damage.

keyTerms.meaning: This is the reason
It is not in your power
That you should make [it] a מועד
My ox

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן says two different תנאים taught the two clauses. רבה keeps the ברייתא as one teaching: custody never changes the status, and in the סיפא the owner simply rejects the מועד status the borrower created. רב פפא gives a third answer in the next step.
steps.whyThisMatters: רבה shows that a ruling which looks like it is about custody may really rest on a different reason: the owner's claim against the borrower.

phrases.english: Rabba said:
Since in the first clause custody does not change [the status],
the last clause too [holds] custody does not change [the status].
And in the last clause, this is the reason –
because he can say to him:
phrases.notes: The owner is the one speaking, and he is talking to the borrower.

phrases.english: It is not in your power
to make my ox forewarned.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה אָמַר: מִדְּרֵישָׁא רְשׁוּת אֵינָהּ מְשַׁנָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to step 12's contradiction, unlike רבי יוחנן's in step 13, without splitting the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Giving the סיפא a different reason so both clauses share one rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The סיפא resets the ox to a תם because the change of custody changes its status.
steps.terutzMaskana: Custody never changes the status. The סיפא's half damage comes from the owner's claim that the borrower could not make his ox a מועד.

steps.title: רב פפא: Custody does change the status, but the owner's name stays on the ox
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא keeps the ברייתא as one teaching, the opposite way from רבה. Both clauses hold that a change of רשות changes the status. In the רישא the ox stays a מועד for a different reason: it is still identified with its owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Since the last clause holds that a change of custody changes the ox's status, the first clause holds this too. The reason the ox stays a מועד in the first clause is that wherever it goes, it is still called by its owner's name.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a third answer to the contradiction between the רישא and the סיפא. He reads both clauses as holding that a change of custody does change the ox's status.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה made the סיפא fit the רישא, so in his reading custody never changes the status. רב פפא does the reverse and makes the רישא fit the סיפא, so custody always changes the status. The רישא is a special case: the ox became a מועד at the owner's house, and it still carries the owner's name even at the borrower's, so for this purpose it never really left his רשות.

keyTerms.meaning: A change of custody changes the ox's legal status
Its owner's name is on it. The ox is still identified with its owner
Since the last clause (says so)

steps.whatToRemember: There are three ways to handle the ברייתא. רבי יוחנן says each clause comes from a different תנא. רבה says custody does not change the status in either clause. רב פפא says custody changes the status in both clauses, but in the רישא the ox stays 'under its owner's name.'

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Since in the last clause a change of custody changes the status,
in the first clause too, a change of custody changes the status;
and in the first clause, this is the reason:
because wherever it goes,
its owner's name is upon it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר: מִדְּסֵיפָא רְשׁוּת מְשַׁנָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third answer to the קשיא of step 12. It is the mirror image of רבה's answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Harmonization: the רישא is read to match the סיפא, and the רישא gets its own special reason
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The רישא seemed to show that custody does not change the status, because the ox stayed a מועד at the borrower's.
steps.terutzMaskana: Custody does change the status. In the רישא the ox stays a מועד only because it is still identified with the owner where it became a מועד.

steps.title: May a stadium ox that killed someone be offered on the altar?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule that a שור האצטדין is not put to death. It then asks whether such an ox is still fit to be a קרבן.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said a stadium ox is not liable to death. The question was asked: what is its status for the altar?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic. It quotes a line from the משנה and asks a question about it, setting up the argument that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A stadium ox is trained to gore, so it is not killed when it kills a person. An ox that killed a person normally cannot be brought on the מזבח, even if it was not put to death. So the question is whether the stadium ox's exemption from death also makes it fit for the מזבח.

keyTerms.meaning: A stadium ox, trained to gore for sport
A question was raised before them (the חכמים)
Regarding the altar, meaning whether it can be a קרבן

phrases.english: A stadium ox
phrases.notes: This line is quoted from our משנה.

phrases.english: is not liable to be put to death.
A question was raised before them:
What is its status regarding the altar?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic based on a different line of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a stadium ox that killed a person is fit or disqualified as a קרבן.

steps.title: רב says fit, שמואל says disqualified
steps.stepSummary: רב rules the ox כשר because it was אנוס, since it only did what it was trained to do. שמואל rules it פסול because a sin was still done through it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: it is fit. שמואל said: it is disqualified. רב says fit because the ox was forced. שמואל says disqualified because a sin was done through it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב and שמואל answer the question in opposite ways. The גמרא then gives the reason behind each opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב looks at the ox: it was trained by people to gore, so it is not to blame. שמואל looks at the act: whether or not the ox is to blame, a person was killed through it, and that is enough to make it פסול for the מזבח.

keyTerms.meaning: Fit to be offered
Disqualified
Forced; acting because of something beyond its control
A sin was done through it

phrases.english: Rav said: It is fit,
and Shmuel said: It is disqualified.
Rav says fit, because it was forced.
And Shmuel says disqualified,
because a sin was done through it.
phrases.notes: The letter in square brackets is added in the corrected wording.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָמַר: כָּשֵׁר, וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: פָּסוּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 16 with a dispute.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב: כשר, because the ox was אנוס. שמואל: פסול, because a sin was done through it.
steps.whyThisMatters: The argument comes down to whether being forced removes the disqualification, or whether the act alone disqualifies. The coming challenge will test שמואל's view.

steps.title: A ברייתא disqualifies a goring animal from the altar
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that reads the words of the פסוק about bringing a קרבן. Each phrase excludes a kind of animal, and the last one excludes the נוגח, an animal that gored. This opens a challenge to שמואל, which is spelled out in step 21.
steps.simpleTranslation: They objected: 'From the animal' excludes an animal that engaged in bestiality and one that was the object of bestiality. 'From the herd' excludes an animal that was worshipped. 'From the flock' excludes an animal set aside for idol worship. 'And from the flock' excludes an animal that gored.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a challenge by quoting a ברייתא. This sets up the attack; how it applies to the stadium ox is worked out in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא derives a list of disqualified animals from the פסוק. The last item is the נוגח, a goring animal. The challenge itself comes from רבי שמעון's comment that follows: with a נוגח, being forced is not treated like acting willingly. That implies a forced goring ox like the stadium ox is fit, against שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal that engaged in bestiality, and one that was the object of it
An animal that was worshipped as a god
An animal set aside for idol worship
An animal that gored and killed a person

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
"From the animal"
comes to exclude an animal that engaged in bestiality and one that was the object of it.
"From the herd" comes to exclude an animal that was worshipped.
"From the flock" comes to exclude an animal set aside for idol worship.
"And from the flock" comes to exclude an animal that gored.
phrases.notes: The extra letter ו ('and') is what teaches this last exclusion.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: ״מִן הַבְּהֵמָה״ – לְהוֹצִיא אֶת הָרוֹבֵעַ וְאֶת הַנִּרְבָּע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a challenge to the dispute in step 17, aimed at שמואל's ruling that the stadium ox is פסול.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that a stadium ox that killed a person is פסול for the מזבח
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא goes on to say that a נוגח acting under אונס is not treated like a willing one. If that refers to קרבנות, a stadium ox, which gores only because it was trained to, is fit, against שמואל. The full force of the challenge is spelled out in step 21.

steps.title: רבי שמעון asks why the Torah lists both the bestiality animal and the goring animal
steps.stepSummary: Inside the ברייתא, רבי שמעון asks why both exclusions are needed, since each one seems to make the other unnecessary.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון said: If the Torah already said a רובע is disqualified, why did it need to say a נוגח is disqualified? And if it said נוגח, why did it need to say רובע?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from the previous step continues. רבי שמעון raises a question that sets up his explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both a רובע and a נוגח are animals that had a sin done through them. So it seems the Torah could have taught one and we would learn the other from it. רבי שמעון asks why the Torah wrote both.

keyTerms.meaning: Why was it said? A question about an extra-seeming phrase

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon said:
If it is stated that an animal used for bestiality is excluded,
why is it stated that a goring animal is excluded?
And if it is stated that a goring animal is excluded,
why is it stated that an animal used for bestiality is excluded?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן: אִם נֶאֱמַר רוֹבֵעַ – לָמָּה נֶאֱמַר נוֹגֵחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues quoting the ברייתא brought in step 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why does the Torah need separate exclusions for a רובע and a נוגח?

steps.title: Each case has a rule the other lacks, so both had to be written
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון answers that a רובע is disqualified even when forced, unlike a נוגח. A נוגח's owner pays כופר, unlike a רובע's owner. So neither can be learned from the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because each case has something the other does not. With a רובע, being forced counts like acting willingly. With a נוגח, being forced does not count like acting willingly. With a נוגח, the owner pays כופר. With a רובע, the owner does not pay כופר. So the Torah had to state both.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון answers his own question. He shows that each case is stricter than the other in some way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A רובע is stricter because it is disqualified even in a case of אונס. So you could not learn the רובע rule from the נוגח. A נוגח is stricter because it brings a payment of כופר. So you could not learn the נוגח rule from the רובע. Each case has its own stricter point, which is why both had to be written.

keyTerms.meaning: Being forced; something beyond one's control
Willingly; by choice
Ransom payment owed by the owner when his ox kills a person
It was necessary to say

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'stricter' does not mean one case is worse overall. It means each case has one specific rule that the other case does not have.

phrases.english: Because there is something with the bestiality animal
that is not true of the goring animal,
and there is something with the goring animal
that is not true of the bestiality animal.
With bestiality, the Torah treated forced like willing,

phrases.aramaic: נוֹגֵחַ – לֹא עָשָׂה בּוֹ אוֹנֶס כְּרָצוֹן.
phrases.english: with goring, the Torah did not treat forced like willing.
With goring, the owner pays ransom,
with bestiality, he does not pay the ransom.
Therefore it was necessary to say bestiality,
and it was necessary to say goring.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי שמעון's question from step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Each case has a unique rule: a רובע is disqualified even when forced, and a נוגח involves כופר. So neither can be learned from the other.

steps.title: The line about forced goring must be about קרבנות, which challenges שמואל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא focuses on the line that a נוגח acting under אונס is not treated like one acting willingly. It suggests this line is about fitness for a קרבן. That would mean a forced goring ox, like the שור האצטדין, is fit, as רב said.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case, the ברייתא teaches that with a רובע, forced is treated like willing, but with a נוגח, forced is not treated like willing. What law is this about? Is it not about bringing it as a קרבן?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a precise inference from רבי שמעון's words. It aims that inference at the argument between רב and שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The context of the ברייתא is which animals may be brought as a קרבן. So the most natural reading is that a נוגח that gored under אונס is not disqualified. A שור האצטדין gores only because it was trained to, which makes it an אונס case. So it would be כשר, just as רב ruled. That goes against שמואל, who ruled it פסול.

keyTerms.meaning: In any case, it teaches: the גמרא is focusing on one specific line
For what law? What practical rule is this about?
Is it not? Introduces the suggested answer

steps.whyThisMatters: This inference is the real force of the ברייתא in the רב-שמואל argument. Whether the אונס line is about קרבנות decides whether שמואל can stand.

phrases.english: In any case, it teaches:
with bestiality, forced was treated like willing,

phrases.aramaic: נוֹגֵחַ – לֹא עָשָׂה בּוֹ אוֹנֶס כְּרָצוֹן.
phrases.english: with goring, forced was not treated like willing.
For what law?
Is it not for a קרבן?

steps.triggerLanguage: קָתָנֵי מִיהַת, רוֹבֵעַ – עָשָׂה בּוֹ אוֹנֶס כְּרָצוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes רבי שמעון's explanation from step 20 and applies it to the argument between רב and שמואל from step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל, who rules a שור האצטדין פסול for a קרבן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says a נוגח under אונס is not treated like a willing one. If this is about קרבנות, a forced goring ox is כשר, which contradicts שמואל.
steps.raayaObject: רב's ruling that a שור האצטדין is כשר
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי שמעון's words in the ברייתא: נוגח – לא עשה בו אונס כרצון

steps.title: The line is about putting the ox to death, not about a קרבן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the line about a forced נוגח deals with whether the ox is put to death, not whether it can be brought as a קרבן.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the line is about the ox being put to death.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the challenge from step 21. The line 'a forced נוגח is not like a willing one' is talking about putting the ox to death, not about using it as a קרבן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 21 the גמרא read the line as saying that a forced goring ox is fit for a קרבן. That would support רב and challenge שמואל. Now the גמרא says the line means something else: a forced goring ox is not killed. So the ברייתא says nothing about קרבן fitness, and שמואל is no longer challenged.

keyTerms.meaning: For killing, meaning whether the ox is put to death
Being forced, acting without its own will
Acting willingly
A stadium ox, trained to gore

phrases.english: No, it is about putting it to death.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21 by moving the line to a different topic.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the topic of the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The line about a forced נוגח was thought to be about fitness for a קרבן, which would make the stadium ox fit, as רב said.
steps.terutzMaskana: The line is about whether the ox is put to death, so it does not decide the argument between רב and שמואל.

steps.title: Proof that the line must be about putting the ox to death
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports its answer. When it comes to קרבנות, the Torah never draws a line between a forced animal and a willing one, so the ברייתא's line must be about putting the ox to death.
steps.simpleTranslation: This also makes sense. If you say the line is about a קרבן, how can it say 'with a נוגח, the Torah did not treat a forced case like a willing one'? Neither the forced case nor the willing case is written there! So isn't it really about putting the ox to death?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its answer from step 22 with a logical proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says 'the Torah did not make forced like willing' for a נוגח. That only makes sense where the Torah actually speaks about the difference. In the פסוק about קרבנות, the Torah just excludes a נוגח and says nothing about forced or willing. So the line must refer to the laws of putting a goring ox to death, where the Torah does deal with how the goring happened.

keyTerms.meaning: So too it is reasonable. A phrase that brings logical support for the answer just given.
It is written in the Torah
Rather, is it not so that... A phrase that pushes to the only reading left

steps.whatToRemember: The line about a forced נוגח is about the ox being put to death, so this ברייתא gives no proof for רב or for שמואל about קרבנות.

phrases.english: So too it is reasonable;
for if you say it is about a קרבן,
[how could it say] 'with a goring animal, [the Torah] did not make'
phrases.notes: This is רבי שמעון's line from step 20.

phrases.english: 'a forced case like a willing one'?!
Its forced case is not written,
and its willing case is not written!
Rather, is it not about putting it to death?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings logical support for the answer in step 22.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that the ברייתא's forced/willing line deals with putting the ox to death.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The wording of the ברייתא itself. The Torah never mentions forced versus willing in the context of קרבנות.

steps.title: Which case of a רובע is exempt from כופר?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes another line of the same ברייתא: a נוגח's owner pays כופר, but a רובע's owner does not. It asks what case this is talking about.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: a goring animal, its owner pays the ransom. An animal used for bestiality, its owner does not pay the ransom. What is the case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic within the same ברייתא. It sets up a question about what case the rule of no כופר for a רובע fits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line comes from רבי שמעון's answer in step 20, where it showed that a רובע cannot be learned from a נוגח. Now the גמרא wants to know what exact situation is meant. The next two steps test the possible cases.

keyTerms.meaning: Ransom money the owner pays when his ox kills a person
An animal that took part in bestiality
What is the case? What are the exact circumstances?

phrases.english: The Master said:
A goring animal: [its owner] pays the ransom,
an animal used for bestiality: [its owner] does not pay the ransom.
What is the case?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: נוֹגֵחַ מְשַׁלֵּם אֶת הַכּוֹפֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the רב and שמואל discussion and examines a different line of the same ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: In what case does the owner of a רובע not pay כופר?

steps.title: If the animal killed her, killing is killing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries the case where the animal did bestiality with a woman and killed her. It rejects this, because a death is a death, and כופר should be owed either way.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it did bestiality with her and killed her, what difference is it to me whether it killed her with its horn or killed her through bestiality?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the first possible case and shows it cannot be right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: כופר is owed because the animal killed a person. If the רובע killed the woman, a person died. It should not matter whether the death came from goring or from bestiality. So the rule of no כופר cannot be talking about a case where she died.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say. A phrase that introduces a possible case in order to test it
What difference is it to me... Used to argue that two cases are really the same
Horn
Bestiality

phrases.english: If you say that it did bestiality with her and killed her,
what difference is it to me if it killed her with its horn,
what difference is it to me if it killed her through bestiality?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the first possible answer to the question in step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the רובע killed the woman
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: כופר depends on a death. How the animal killed should not matter.

steps.title: If the animal did not kill her, the rule teaches nothing about a רובע
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries the case where the animal did bestiality but did not kill. That fails too. There is no כופר simply because nobody died, so the rule has nothing to do with being a רובע.
steps.simpleTranslation: But rather, if it did bestiality with her and did not kill her, then the reason he does not pay ransom is just that it did not kill her!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the second possible case and shows that it also fails. The next step, אביי's answer, resolves the question of step 24.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If no one died, there is obviously no כופר, whether the animal gored or did bestiality. Then the ברייתא's contrast between a נוגח and a רובע would teach nothing special about a רובע. Both possible cases have now failed, so the גמרא still needs to explain the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: But rather. Introduces the next option after the first was rejected
Because of

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא is not wrong. The גמרא is only showing that the two simple cases do not work, so it will need to find a different explanation.

phrases.english: But rather, that it did bestiality with her and did not kill her?
This, that he does not pay ransom,
is because it did not kill her!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first case failed in step 25, tests the second case and rejects it too.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the רובע did not kill the woman
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Without a death there is never כופר, so the exemption has nothing to do with the animal being a רובע. The ברייתא's contrast would be pointless.

steps.title: אביי: The woman was executed by בית דין
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the ברייתא is talking about an animal that did bestiality with a woman and did not kill her, after which בית דין executed her. He begins to explain why we might have thought כופר is owed.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: The case really is where the animal did bestiality with her and did not kill her. But she was then brought to בית דין, and they executed her. You might have said...
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the problem from step 26 by giving a case where the woman does end up dead, but at the hands of בית דין rather than the animal. The words "מהו דתימא" set up the next move, where he will explain the mistake the ברייתא is coming to prevent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 26 the case of "bestiality without killing" was rejected because nobody died, so there was no reason to mention כופר. אביי keeps that case but adds that בית דין later executed the woman, so there is now a death connected to the animal's act. That gives the ברייתא a real point when it says the owner does not pay כופר.

keyTerms.meaning: Actually, really. It signals going back to an option that was set aside earlier.
It (the animal) did bestiality with her
The court (בית דין)
They executed her
You might have said. It introduces a mistaken idea that the ruling is coming to reject.

steps.confusionAlert: Here it is not the animal that kills the woman. בית דין executes her for the sin. Keep these two kinds of death apart.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Actually, it is where it did bestiality with her and did not kill her,
where they brought her to court and they executed her;
you might have said

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: לְעוֹלָם דְּרַבְעַהּ וְלָא קַטְלַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the rejection in step 26 by adding a detail to that same case: the woman was later executed by בית דין.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (adding a new detail to a case that was already rejected)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: In the case of bestiality without killing, nobody dies, so there is no reason for the ברייתא to mention כופר.
steps.terutzMaskana: Someone does die, since בית דין executed the woman. So the ברייתא has to tell us that the owner still does not pay כופר. The reasoning continues after "מהו דתימא".
